papers.title: Sc-HistoMorphomics: A General Framework for High-throughput, Multimodal Profiling of Nuclear Morphology in Tissues.
papers.abstract: Quantitative cellular morphology provides a rich but underutilized window into cell identity and state. We introduce sc-HistoMorphomics, a scalable framework for profiling nuclear morphology in whole-slide H&E images and correlating these measurements with spatial transcriptomics data. Our pipeline combines deep-learning based segmentation with 194 interpretable morphometric features capturing nuclear shape, eosin and hematoxylin texture, and neighbourhood architecture, enabling high-throughput, multimodal characterization of tissue organization. Applied to endometrium, breast cancer tissue, and pancreas, sc-HistoMorphomics revealed conserved high-dimensional feature structure across tissues and reproducible association between morphology and gene expression. Eosin-based texture features were associated with senescence signatures in endometrium, and morphology-based clustering recapitulated broad stromal, lymphocyte, and epithelial tumor cell classes in breast cancer. In pancreas, negative correlations between CDKN1A and multiple morphological features were consistent across cell types and donors. Together, these results establish sc-HistoMorphomics as a generalizable and interpretable tool for linking morphology with spatially resolved molecular state across diverse tissues.

papers.title: DRAFT: graph-recurrent learning of dynamic gene regulatory networks along single-cell multi-omics trajectories
papers.abstract: Single-cell multi-omics data offer an opportunity to resolve how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are rewired during cell-fate transitions, but most existing methods infer static snapshots, ignore temporal dependencies or assume linear regulation. Here we present DRAFT, a deep learning framework that combines graph attention with recurrent temporal memory to infer dynamic GRNs from time-resolved single-cell multi-omics data. On simulated data, DRAFT outperforms existing methods in accuracy and temporal smoothness. In mouse cellular reprogramming and Drosophila adult spermatogenesis, it recovers interactions supported by independent ChIP-seq, perturbation and Hi-C data, together with known stage-specific regulators. By inferring regulatory activity from dynamic network structure rather than expression alone, DRAFT identifies regulators whose activity precedes their transcriptional peak, including the candidate early germline regulator Mondo. Germline-specific Mondo knockdown alters germline stem cell number and expression of the predicted targets kuz and mamo. DRAFT also enables nonlinear alignment of co-developing lineages and reveals stage-specific cell-cell communication.

papers.title: Vocabulary recurrence, rather than biological grounding, explains tokenization transfer in protein function prediction.
papers.abstract: Sequence-based protein function prediction requires a choice of tokenization. K-mers, the common default, correspond to no biological unit; enzymatic digestion offers a principled alternative, since tryptic peptides are the fragments proteases generate and mass spectrometry measures. We asked whether this grounding improves transfer to unseen proteins. Using six Gene Ontology terms and 23,723 UniProt proteins, we compared tryptic peptides, peptide topics (groups of related peptides), 3-mers, and amino- acid composition, with ESM-2 embeddings and homology transfer as reference points. Peptide performance followed vocabulary coverage: 92.2% of peptide tokens in test proteins were never seen in training, whereas almost every 3-mer had been seen. As a result, 38.9% of test proteins contained no peptide the model had seen, and with nothing to work from, the classifier gave all of them the same answer. The remaining 61.1% of proteins were classified almost perfectly with a random forest; however, because of this uncovered fraction, tryptic peptides scored lower overall than 3-mers under all three classifiers tested (macro-F1 0.640 against 0.690). These results suggest that vocabulary recurrence matters more than biological grounding for tokenization transfer.

papers.title: Elflow: Automated Quality Control and Self-Supervised Representation Learning for High-Dimensional Cytometry
papers.abstract: High-dimensional flow and mass cytometry are foundational technologies for clinical immunophenotyping and hematological diagnostics, yet computational data analysis remains bottlenecked by operator-subjective manual gating. While computational tools have emerged, they remain fragmented across isolated tasks such as quality control or discrete clustering, leaving an unmet need for integrated, modular workflows that resolve continuous biological variation without manual supervision. Here, we introduce Elflow, a modular, self-supervised framework that links automated quality control, single-cell representation learning, and patient-level modeling without manual gating at inference. Elflow couples automated machine-learning quality control with Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization (VICReg) to learn continuous, batch-resilient single-cell representations without negative pairs or hand-labeled training sets. Across four diverse public benchmarks, Elflow adapts to distinct biological panels and clinical objectives. On 22-channel spectral flow cytometry (OMIP-030), self-supervised embeddings preserve fine functional T-cell gradations and outperform classical baselines in unsupervised clustering, while an anchor-guided extension accurately reproduces canonical manual gating hierarchies. On hand-curated CyTOF panels (Levine-13), linear PCA matches deep models, establishing an empirical boundary condition where linear methods suffice. Across multi-center clinical cohorts (FlowCAP-II), Elflow representations achieve high diagnostic sensitivity for acute myeloid leukemia across heterogeneous instruments despite severe class imbalance. In longitudinal immune monitoring (FlowCAP-IV), patient mean embeddings and micro-cluster differential histograms preserve rare antigen-specific responses, yielding significant AIDS-free survival stratification. By uniting automated quality control, self-supervised representation learning, and multi-scale patient aggregation, Elflow provides a modular, reproducibly benchmarked framework for high-parameter and multi-center translational cytometry.

papers.title: BI-SCUDO Regression - A novel algorithm to infer clinical variables from omics datasets
papers.abstract: Regression analysis of high-throughput omics data is often made difficult by noise, batch effects, and the loss of information resulting from the discretization of continuous variables. Existing machine learning algorithms often struggle to extract stable biological signals under these heterogeneous conditions. We introduce BI-SCUDO Regression, a rank-based regression framework designed for omics data analysis. By leveraging within-sample rankings and network-based predictions, BI-SCUDO Regression bypasses the need for complex normalization and provides robust, interpretable results. In synthetic benchmarks, BI-SCUDO Regression demonstrated strong resilience to noise, maintaining predictive and feature-selection stability under conditions in which standard models exhibited performance degradation. When applied to cohorts from TCGA datasets, BI-SCUDO Regression consistently outperformed LASSO, Random Forest Regression, and XGBoost in predicting survival, with an average increase in Ratio of Performance to Deviation ranging from 43% to 86%, depending on the comparator. Furthermore, the algorithm consistently identified parsimonious, statistically significant, and biologically relevant biomarkers, with enrichment for cancer-related terms across all stage stratifications. Although BI-SCUDO Regression incurs higher training times due to its genetic optimization strategy, it offers a robust and interpretable approach to outcome prediction and biomarker discovery, with potential applications in precision medicine, where noisy data compromise the performance of conventional regression methods.

papers.title: scUNVEIL: Learning scRNA-seq Cell Embeddings Through Measurement Enrichment
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretraining can improve scRNA-seq representations through measurement enrichment: estimating what the same measurement would reveal at greater UMI depth under the same measurement process. We introduce scUNVEIL, a self-supervised model trained through next-UMI prediction. We show that the Bayes-optimal next-UMI predictor is the posterior mean of the transcriptome composition that arbitrarily deep sequencing would reveal. Because UMI identities are exchangeable conditional on transcriptome composition, scUNVEIL operates directly on count vectors using a residual multilayer perceptron, without attention over gene tokens. The measurement-enriched transcriptome composition is predicted from a single low-dimensional hidden state, which therefore serves naturally as the cell embedding. The same model provides both reusable cell representations and measurement-enriched gene-expression estimates. scUNVEIL was pretrained without labels or auxiliary metadata on approximately 92 million human cells spanning diverse tissues. Under linear evaluation on fine-grained cell-type annotation, its zero-shot representations achieved the best performance among the evaluated methods, while providing over 1000-fold faster inference than the strongest evaluated transformer-based foundation model and matching that model's predictive performance using 88% fewer input UMIs per cell. Further evaluations show that these representations improve prediction of tumor reactivity, mitochondrial membrane potential, cell morphology, and lineage-associated treatment outcomes.

papers.title: GENECraft: A Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System for Controllable Regulatory DNA Design
papers.abstract: Designing regulatory DNA requires reconciling two complementary modeling paradigms: genomic language models (gLMs) capture evolutionary syntax without guaranteeing targeted regulatory activity, whereas sequence-to-function predictors provide explicit functional supervision without enforcing native-like sequence plausibility. We introduce GENECraft, a training-free Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System (FP-DDS) that couples a genomic language model (Carbon) and a functional oracle (AlphaGenome) during inference-time optimization to balance predicted regulatory activity and consistency with genomic sequence priors. GENECraft evolves continuous latent nucleotide logits while evaluating strictly decoded discrete DNA sequences under a time-dependent composite vector field that fuses normalized functional utility, bidirectional contextual prior guidance, and compositional quality penalties, followed by feasibility-first trajectory readout. Across 2,185 loci spanning promoters, multi-constraint enhancers, and 18 transcription factors (TFs), GENECraft achieves full-joint success rates of 62.70%, 65.23%, and 94.56% (macro-averaged), substantially outperforming seven optimization, evolutionary, and generative baselines (which reach at most 2.15% on enhancers). In matched 336-locus ablations, in-loop Carbon guidance reduces native-relative dinucleotide divergence by 7.8--11.5%, enhancer context sensitivity by 10.5%, and TF mutation sensitivity by 11.0%, establishing FP-DDS as a principled framework for controllable regulatory DNA design.

papers.title: Accurate and interpretable protein complex stoichiometry prediction through agentic AI with StoiAgent
papers.abstract: Accurate protein complex structure modeling requires knowledge of complex stoichiometry, yet the copy numbers of individual subunits are often unknown. Consequently, predicting protein complex stoichiometry has emerged as a major challenge in recent years. Here, we present StoiAgent, a large language model (LLM)-powered AI agent that automates the retrieval and integration of sequence, structural, and literature evidence to predict stoichiometry while preserving interpretable reasoning traces (chain of thoughts) of its evidence assessment and ranking decision. An open-weight LLM model, Qwen3.6-27B, is used by StoiAgent as the LLM backbone to combine sequences, structural templates, AlphaFold3 structure predictions, and literature evidence, and perform stoichiometry candidate generation and ranking. On 56 CASP17 protein complex targets, it achieves top-1 accuracy of 75.0%, which represents a 23.2 percentage-point improvement over PreStoi with AlphaFold3 ranking (51.8%) and matches the top-1 accuracy of StoPred. Moreover, StoiAgent has a higher top-3 and top-5 accuracy than StoPred (85.7% versus 80.4% and 87.5% versus 85.7%, respectively). Furthermore, it outperforms general-purpose frontier LLMs, including ChatGPT and Gemini, in stoichiometry prediction. Case studies further illustrate how StoiAgent evaluates competing assembly hypotheses by integrating complementary evidence, with recorded reasoning traces documenting its decision-making process. Overall, StoiAgent demonstrates the potential of LLM-powered AI agents to improve protein complex stoichiometry prediction through the automated integration of diverse sources of evidence while providing interpretable explanations to guide downstream structure modeling.

papers.title: CAS-X: A Probabilistic Multi-Tissue eQTL Framework for Prioritizing Candidate Effector Genes at Type 2 Diabetes Risk Loci
papers.abstract: The genetic etiology of Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) involves regulatory mechanisms operating across multiple metabolic tissues. However, candidate effector gene prioritization can be limited by approaches that focus predominantly on pancreatic transcriptomics. To address this limitation, we developed CAS-X, a computational multi-tissue functional genomics framework for prioritizing candidate effector genes at T2D susceptibility loci. CAS-X integrates fine-mapped Posterior Inclusion Probabilities (PIP) and allelic fold changes (aFC) across five tissues: pancreas, skeletal muscle, subcutaneous adipose, visceral adipose, and whole blood. In the reported analysis, multi-tissue integration identified 28 candidate genes meeting the selected prioritization threshold, compared with 12 under the pancreas-only baseline, representing a 133.3% increase in candidate coverage. Prioritized candidates included JAZF1, FTO, GRB14, and CDKN2B. Framework robustness was examined through Leave-One-Tissue-Out sensitivity analysis and comparisons with non-metabolic GTEx Brain Cortex controls. Pathway enrichment analysis highlighted associations with insulin resistance, adipocytokine signaling, and lipolysis regulation. The analysis also incorporated phenome-wide associations and computational assessments of therapeutic tractability. CAS-X provides a computational approach for integrating regulatory evidence across metabolic tissues to support candidate effector gene prioritization in T2D research.

papers.title: CATEomics: model selection and ensembling for heterogeneous treatment effect estimation from high-dimensional omics data
papers.abstract: CATEomics addresses the lack of a standardized and reproducible process for choosing among conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimators in high-dimensional omics studies, where their estimation errors cannot be evaluated directly from observed outcomes. The R package accepts a SummarizedExperiment, applies common preprocessing and data partitions across R and Python estimators, compares their out-of-fold estimates using proxy losses, supports model selection and ensembling, and returns the resulting CATE estimates to the original object for downstream omics analysis. Availability and implementation: CATEomics is implemented in R and is freely available under the MIT license at https://github.com/matsui-lab/CATEomics. The software version described here (v0.99.0) is archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24189754. A vignette illustrates the complete workflow from a SummarizedExperiment to downstream analysis.

papers.title: Gene set selection for classification with single-cell RNA-seq
papers.abstract: Marker genes are important for analyzing and interpreting single-cell RNA-seq (scRNAseq) experiments. They are used to identify and categorize cell types and can also be useful for the design of downstream experiments. We present CellSieve, which tackles the problem of finding effective gene sets rather than distilling markers one at a time. While several "combinatorial" approaches to gene set selection have been proposed, we find that our approach, which leverages a combination of multinomial logistic regression and linear programming, is much more effective at finding small gene sets that can classify cell types.

papers.title: Flux Transformer learns intracellular metabolic fluxes from isotope labeling and measured reaction rates
papers.abstract: Cells convert incoming nutrients into energy and biomass via metabolic fluxes. Quantifying these fluxes involves feeding cells isotope-labeled nutrients, quantifying metabolite labeling patterns, and inverting the labeling data to retrieve the underlying flux distribution. Traditional metabolic flux analysis (MFA) is both computationally expensive and frequently requires manual refinement of the cost function to obtain plausible results. For this reason, MFA has remained inaccessible to non-experts. Here we present Flux Transformer, an AI model that uses reaction-specific attention to integrate isotope-labeling data with available reaction-rate measurements, reconstructing mass-balanced steady-state fluxes. The model is trained on simulated data with added noise and identifies the underlying fluxes from these data more effectively than traditional MFA. Provided experimental data from wild-type and mutant bacteria, yeast, plants, and mammalian T cells, it efficiently and accurately recovers expert-curated MFA fluxes. By making flux analysis accessible, Flux Transformer is poised to accelerate metabolic research and engineering.

papers.title: Identifying disease-associated dysbiosis in image-based spatial microbiome via MiSA
papers.abstract: Background: Extensive studies have revealed the associations of microbiome dysbiosis with disease through compositional analysis of 16S rRNA amplicon or shotgun metagenomic sequencing data. However, dysbiosis in spatial organization of microbiome inhabiting the body sites and its implication for diseases remain understudied. Recently developed high phylogenetic resolution fluorescence in situ hybridization (HiPR-FISH) is an image-based mapping technology that provides spatial microbiome data at single-cell resolution, which allows for visualizing and quantifying spatial arrangement of microbial cells. Despite the growing availability of such data, no methods have been tailored to studying spatial dysbiosis in image-based microbiome data. Results: Here we introduce MiSA (Microbiome Spatial Aberration), the first statistical framework for identifying disease-associated spatial dysbiosis and the individual taxa that may contribute to it, based on differing degrees of clustering or regularity, i.e., microbial cells being more aggregated or more evenly spaced than expected under complete spatial randomness, between diagnostic groups. In simulations based on a real dataset, MiSA was robust across diverse and noisy spatial configurations, achieving substantially higher statistical power than a method borrowed from spatial proteomics, while controlling type I error at both the individual-taxon and community levels. When applied to an oral biofilm study, MiSA detected peri-implant mucositis-associated spatial dysbiosis at the community level and identified five taxa as potential contributors, including Actinomyces, which showed increased clustering in mucositis. Conclusions: MiSA is a powerful and robust framework for identifying spatial dysbiosis and the contributing taxa in image-based microbiome data, offering new insights into the spatial organization of microbial communities in disease.

papers.title: Stress granule transcript contrasts between colorectal cancer compartments depend on scoring and depth
papers.abstract: Stress granule (SG) gene-set scores summarize transcription associated with stress-response machinery, but their stability across scoring definitions is uncertain. We compared fibroblast-epithelial expression contrasts for four fixed SG lists in two colorectal cancer single-cell cohorts containing 195,527 cells from 85 donors. Analyses used donor pairing, gene-wise standardized expression, within-cell ranks and raw-count pseudobulk summaries, with tissue and sequencing-depth sensitivities. At least 20 tumor cells per compartment were available for 15 and 29 paired donors. Pseudobulk SG-A contrasts were negative in both cohorts: median differences in mean log2 counts per million were -0.383 (95% confidence interval -0.493 to -0.319) and -0.493 (-0.614 to -0.384). Rank-based SG-B contrasts were also negative in both cohorts. In a post hoc comparison using identical depth-retained cells and weights, the second cohort had positive gene-Z estimates and negative rank-based estimates; the positive estimates did not meet the eight-test false-discovery threshold. Spatial comparisons depended on the fibroblast reference subtype, and the CosMx panel measured only 11 of 27 SG-B genes. RNA-protein correlations varied across genes, while organoid depletion calls were more frequent for selected translation-associated members than for the four core members. These findings establish reproducible relative-expression contrasts under specified definitions and show that their direction can change across scoring and depth conditions. Reporting the scoring definition, retained donor population, depth sensitivity and gene coverage together identifies the contrasts that reproduce and provides a defined basis for testing their relationship to SG formation.

papers.title: TS-Zarr: a cloud-optimized Zarr layout for viewing and analyzing biomedical time series
papers.abstract: Background: Biomedical time series are recorded at high sampling rates for hours to days across tens to hundreds of channels. Each recording occupies gigabytes to terabytes of storage. FAIR data sharing requirements often place recordings in cloud storage. Visual analysis requires downsampling windows wider than a few seconds to the pixel width of the screen. Visualization tools therefore either read a local copy of the recording or query a dedicated resampling server in front of the data. Findings: We present TS-Zarr, a Zarr v3 layout for time series data. It stores the samples of each channel alongside a pyramid of summary statistics at progressively coarser levels. Zarr on cloud storage offers low-latency, high-throughput parallel reads. The layout lets a reader fetch only the channels and windows it needs. These targeted reads scale better than the same reads from HDF5 and EDF. Precomputed levels trade additional storage and error-bound signal transformation for faster and more scalable visual analysis that moves from the whole recording to narrow windows. As users grow and windows widen, precomputed reads from cloud storage scale beyond the point at which a resampling server fails. Conclusions: Precomputed levels let researchers visualize a recording without downloading a local copy or querying a dedicated resampling server. The time to read a view remains bounded as the window under view widens. Zarr on cloud storage also provides efficient, highly parallelizable, targeted reads of raw sample data for analysis.

papers.title: MetaboRx: R Shiny application for quality assessment and preprocessing of mass spectrometry-based metabolomics data
papers.abstract: Introduction Metabolomics datasets offer deep insights into biological systems, yet the multi-step analytical workflow, from sample preparation through instrumental analysis, introduces unwanted variation. This variation, including signal drift and batch effects can confound true biological signals. Although rigorous quality control (QC) and data preprocessing are prerequisites for downstream analysis, existing workflows are often fragmented, time-consuming, and inaccessible to non-experts. Objectives To develop a user-friendly software tool for rapid quality assessment and rigorous preprocessing of metabolomics feature tables. Methods MetaboRx is an R Shiny application that integrates orthogonal quality metrics into a single workflow, enabling systematic and transparent evaluation of metabolomics data before and after preprocessing. The application identifies formatting errors and analytically unreliable features and provides flexible preprocessing and visualization options. Results MetaboRx is freely available at https://github.com/ETaylorLab/MetaboRx. Using a semi-targeted LC-MS metabolomics dataset from mouse plasma, perturbed with simulated low-quality data, we demonstrate how MetaboRx facilitates detection of data quality problems, reduces unwanted variation, and prepares data for downstream analysis. Conclusion MetaboRx streamlines metabolomics data quality assessment and preprocessing through an interactive and integrated workflow. The application may improve consistency and reproducibility in metabolomics studies by supporting informed preprocessing decisions and transparent reporting of QC outcomes prior to downstream analysis.

papers.title: EvoRx: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Antibiotic Resistance in Escherichia coli Using Genomic Features
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) complicates bacterial infection management, motivating genomic approaches to predicting antibiotic susceptibility. This study assessed the predictive performance and generalisability of machine-learning models using resistance-associated genomic features from Escherichia coli. Publicly available genomic and phenotypic records yielded 446 genomes, 252 binary genomic features and 1,935 susceptibility observations across nine antibiotics. Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers were compared using validation ROC-AUC, followed by evaluation on held-out test subsets. Additional analyses examined identical genomic feature profiles across partitions, performance across source publications and feature redundancy. Ampicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole achieved held-out accuracies of 93.98% and 93.59%, ROC-AUC values of 0.912 and 0.954, and resistant-isolate recall of 95.16% and 94.55%, respectively. In contrast, ceftazidime achieved 88.52% accuracy and 0.940 ROC-AUC but identified only 22.22% of resistant isolates. Seventy-four held-out observations shared identical 252-feature profiles with training isolates; all were correctly classified. After excluding overlapping observations without retraining, ROC-AUC decreased from 0.912 to 0.848 for ampicillin and from 0.954 to 0.901 for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Exploratory cross-publication evaluations showed variable performance, with shared multilocus sequence types in 16 of 18 comparisons. Reducing genomic features did not materially alter validation performance in the two antibiotics examined. These findings indicate that genomic predictors can discriminate resistance phenotypes, but aggregate accuracy may obscure poor resistant-isolate detection. The findings also distinguish performance on conventionally held-out isolates from performance on previously unseen resistance-feature profiles, an important consideration when bacterial population structure and correlated determinants substantially influence model evaluation. Independent phylogenetic and prospective validation remains necessary before clinical use.

papers.title: AlphaGenome 2 predicts regulatory activity and variant effects across cell states
papers.abstract: Most genetic variants associated with human traits and diseases lie in non-coding DNA, where they can alter gene regulation in specific cell types and states. Single-cell atlases chart these states across tissues and development, but rarely profile enough donors to associate variants with expression directly. Deep learning models could bridge this gap by predicting variant effects from DNA sequence, yet they poorly distinguish related cell states and require fine-tuning for new datasets. Here we present AlphaGenome 2 (AG2), which substantially advances cell-type-specific prediction of regulatory activity and variant effects for gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Trained on organism-wide human and mouse single-cell atlases and bulk functional genomics data, AG2 takes as input a 1-Mb DNA sequence and a condition specifying a target tissue, cell type, or cell state. Conditioning enables AG2 to impute unmeasured epigenomic tracks and predict multimodal variant effects across cell types. Inferring this condition directly from gene expression extends AG2 to unseen datasets and cell states without fine-tuning. AG2 outperforms fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1 and specialized models trained on target datasets, doubling recall of causal single-cell eQTLs at 90% precision. AG2 also achieves state-of-the-art enhancer-gene linking and can pinpoint causal variants at complex trait loci. Across hundreds of human cell types, we generated an atlas of enhancer-gene links and scores for 7 million common variants. As single-cell profiling expands across development, tissues, and disease cohorts, AG2 provides a blueprint for turning observational atlases into variant effect maps.

papers.title: Evaluating local assembly strategies for human long-read structural variant calling
papers.abstract: Long-read sequencing enables detection of structural variants (SVs) with far greater accuracy and completeness than was previously possible. This advance has spurred the development of many SV callers that implement diverse algorithmic strategies. Commonly, SV calling proceeds in several processing steps. Evaluations of SV callers, however, typically focus on overall performance and conceal which steps drive observed differences. This hinders targeted, evidence-based improvements to existing SV calling approaches. Here, we implemented five consensus computation strategies similar to those employed by popular SV callers that perform a local assembly. We compare their outputs on extensive simulated and real data and reveal that some strategies are more effective for particular input data types. For example, the strategy employed by PacBio's tool Sawfish works very well on HiFi reads and recent ONT data, but fails on the older and noisier ONT reads. While the read error profiles and the read pre-processing has a substantial influence on some strategies, other strategies are more robust overall. These findings guide algorithmic decisions for the development of improved future SV callers.

papers.title: statLens enables accurate and interpretable statistical intelligence
papers.abstract: Diverse existing approaches and analyses of large-scale biomedical omics datasets along with the complexity of the corresponding statistical analytical workflows pose challenges to the direct application of large language models (LLMs) to data analysis tasks. We present statLens, a model-agnostic AI-driven statistical intelligence framework that integrates LLMs, code and human review. We demonstrate statLens using differential expression analysis across heterogeneous biomedical data as a use case. On 102 benchmark tasks from 74 datasets across six omics modalities, statLens maintained consistently high accuracy (92.5--95.0%) across seven language models and outperformed LLM-only inference (17.5--46.8%), whereas autonomous-agent accuracy varied widely (58.7--99.5%). We also showed that statLens substantially improved the accuracy of the four small language models (92.5--94.4%) over autonomous agents (58.7--92.2%) and LLM-only inference (17.5--43.5%). By decomposing analytical workflows into complementary tasks for code, LLMs and human experts, statLens provides an integrated framework for more accurate, interpretable and reproducible AI-assisted data analysis, particularly in complex omics settings.

papers.title: SpaceMACE: Spatially-Aware Tumour Cell Annotation for Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Accurate discrimination between tumour and non-tumour cells is essential for interpreting spatial transcriptomics data and identifying spatially resolved therapeutic targets. Existing tumour-cell annotation approaches were primarily developed for single-cell RNA sequencing and do not explicitly incorporate the spatial organization of cells. Here, we introduce SpaceMACE, an extension of the MACE tumour-cell annotation framework for sequencing-based and imaging-based spatial transcriptomics. SpaceMACE first combines reference-based cell-type classification with copy-number-variation-based tumour classification. The resulting consensus annotations are subsequently refined using spatial proximity and gene-expression similarity. We evaluated SpaceMACE across multiple spatial transcriptomics platforms, including Stereo-seq, Visium HD, CosMx and Xenium, and across colorectal, hepatocellular and ovarian cancer datasets. SpaceMACE retained the high precision of the original MACE framework while improving the spatial coherence of tumour-cell annotations. Together, these results demonstrate that SpaceMACE provides a scalable and platform-independent framework for tumour-cell annotation in spatial transcriptomics and supports the spatial investigation of tumour-specific molecular targets.

papers.title: Measuring Phylogenetic Information Content Based on Clade Support
papers.abstract: Phylogenetic information content is often understood as the degree to which data lend support to hypotheses about the monophyly of clades. This is most commonly expressed in terms of clade support, typically estimated by resampling techniques such as the bootstrap and the jackknife. Here, I discuss how to summarize this aspect of data quality. I show that raw bootstrap or jackknife proportions are unsuitable for this purpose and instead suggest a logarithmic transformation, which can be interpreted as translating the clade support values to the number of characters expected to give the same resampling proportion in parsimony analysis of a homoplasy-free data matrix. The distribution of the number of these "supporting characters" and descriptive statistics derived from this distribution, such as the mean (Mean Character Support, or MCS) and its standard deviation, provide powerful summaries of the quality of the underlying data set. I demonstrate for both empirical and simulated data sets that MCS accurately reflects information content, and that some popular alternative measures of data quality (the ensemble consistency index, the ensemble retention index, data decisiveness and the total support index) do not. Unlike most other measures of data quality, MCS can be applied to trees resulting from a range of alternative phylogenetic methods, including parsimony, distance and maximum likelihood approaches.

papers.title: Policy-Enforced Genomic Repositories and Institutional Data Governance for African Pathogen Surveillance with UbuntuBio
papers.abstract: Research centers curating pathogen sequence cohorts often operate under constrained bandwidth, multi-institutional data-sharing agreements, and strict biosafety requirements. Global public archives keep released sequences permanently open, external viral portals enforce terms outside local institutional custody, and standard Git Large File Storage (LFS) duplicates identical binaries across repositories without validating taxonomy or geography. We present UbuntuBio (v1.0.0), a Git-native, policy-enforced genomic repository platform deployed at https://ubuntubio.org and developed at the West African Centre for Cell Biology of Infectious Pathogens (WACCBIP), University of Ghana. UbuntuBio integrates four mechanisms under a single storage root: (1) bare Git repositories storing dataset cards, sample sheets, and approximately 130-byte LFS pointers backed by prefix-sharded SHA-256 content-addressed storage (CAS) with visibility-scoped wire deduplication; (2) a four-phase commit pipeline recoverable via cross-plane reconciliation that enforces 55 African Union country codes against offline Natural Earth polygons, core MIxS-derived fields, Taxon 9606 rejection, and server-keyed targeted human-marker screening identically across HTTP commits and Git pre-receive hooks; (3) institutional custody controls combining Data Use Agreements (DUAs), revocable 900-second RS256 capability tokens, key rotation, tamper-evident hash-chained logs, and externally anchorable RS256 audit checkpoints; and (4) an embedded SQLite WAL and FTS5 catalog filtered by access tier. In single-node evaluation, UbuntuBio classified 18/18 policy boundary fixtures consistently across Python, Git, and HTTP paths; showed 0/265,157 false cross-matches on 21/22 RefSeq pathogen sequences (while cross-matching Candida albicans 18S rDNA at 0.113% and Chlorocebus sabaeus Alu repeats in ENA stool reads, confirming targeted marker detection rather than verified human DNA decontamination); matched conditional uniform (n = 2,000; 200-seed 0.01% convergence 19.0% vs. 18.13% expected) and interior (n = 1,000) detection theory while detecting all spike-ins at [≥] 0.5% (30/30); halved two-repository disk usage on 613.83 MiB Nigerian E. coli runs; passed 27/27 structured-filter correctness checks over 10,000 biosamples and reached graded NDCG@10 = 0.920 on independent free-text BM25 queries with zero private leaks; and recovered cleanly across seven injected phase-transition faults.

papers.title: Generative Data Augmentation for Small-Cohort Glioblastoma Diagnosis from Circulating microRNA: Why Same-Modality Validation Overstates Performance
papers.abstract: Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) have potential as minimally invasive biomarkers for glioblastoma (GBM), but the small size of discovery groups makes it difficult to develop a classifier. The discovery cohort, GSE122488, comprised 38 patients (n = 38). Generative data augmentation was applied to increase the dataset, although evaluations based on held-out samples from the same cohort or a single validation set make it difficult to distinguish biological signals from cohort- or platform-specific effects. CTGAN and Tabular Variational Autoencoder (TVAE) models were trained on the 38-patient cohort producing 500 synthetic samples each. Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers were trained on augmented datasets and assessed using an escalating validation approach: first on an independent plasma cohort of the same modality (GSE184472, n = 118), and then on a tissue cohort from a different platform (Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas (CGGA), n = 198). XGBoost using TVAE-augmented data achieved an AUROC of 0.59 (95% CI 0.49-0.70) on GSE184472, compared with 0.42 to 0.53 without augmentation, although no AUROC on this cohort was significantly different from chance. However, this improvement did not carry to CGGA, where AUROC was 0.40 (95% CI 0.32-0.48) before harmonisation and 0.47 after Min-Max harmonisation. After harmonisation, a recall of 1.00 resulted from predicting every sample as GBM, leading to an accuracy of 0.41 and showing poor discrimination. The generalisation gap was examined in terms of modality mismatch, differing class definitions between cohorts, synthetic-data-related class imbalance, and incomplete cross-platform harmonisation. These findings show the need for independent, cross-platform validation before using data augmentation for diagnosis. The escalating validation framework provides a way to evaluate generalizability in small-cohort studies.

papers.title: Deciphering the Biological Function of Tandem Mass Spectra Using a Dual-Modal Metabolite Language Model
papers.abstract: Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry untargeted metabolomics captures thousands of metabolic peaks from biological samples. Conventional identification-dependent metabolomics workflows require confident structural annotation before identified features can enter downstream pathway or functional analysis. However, only a small fraction of detected metabolic features can be assigned confident structural annotations, leaving a large fraction difficult to incorporate into downstream biological interpretation, a form of "functional dark matter". Here, we introduce Spec2Function, a function-centric framework that infers biological functions from tandem mass spectrometry (MS2) spectra. Spec2Function is trained using characterized spectrum-text pairs but does not require prior structural identification of the query spectra at inference time. At its core is Spec2Biotext, a dual-encoder contrastive model that embeds MS2 spectra and curated multi-aspect natural language functional texts into a unified functional space. Combined with a retrieval-augmented generation framework grounded in curated databases and biomedical literature, Spec2Function retrieves evidence-grounded biological knowledge and produces coherent functional summaries for individual spectra or groups of spectra. Across metabolite- and pathway-level benchmarks, Spec2Function achieved higher similarity to reference functional descriptions than the evaluated comparators and expanded the fraction of the metabolome accessible to functional interpretation. Application to a human liver cirrhosis cohort recapitulated known metabolic alterations and identified additional literature-supported functional modules. Applying Spec2Function to a 30-organ macaque aging atlas revealed organ-specific metabolic functions and previously unreported functional modules that were supported by independent human and mouse datasets. Together, these results position Spec2Function as a function-centric framework for scalable biological interpretation of structurally unannotated MS2 spectra.

papers.title: Automated segmentation of renal structures using brightfield images of unstained kidney biopsies
papers.abstract: The automated segmentation of unstained kidney brightfield microscopy images remains a significant challenge in medical imaging. In conventional histopathology, staining provides crucial structural and molecular contrast, allowing renal compartments and structures to be readily distinguished. The absence of staining markedly reduces this contrast, obscuring the fine architectural details that are essential for diagnosis. Addressing this gap would reduce reliance on staining protocols, reduce technical and interpretive variability, and preserve valuable tissue for downstream molecular or multi-omics analyses. Ultimately, automation of unstained image segmentation could enable faster, more objective tissue analysis while preserving samples for further molecular testing. In this work, we provide a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art segmentation methods applied to renal brightfield microscopy images. Current findings highlight a predominance of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based architectures for semantic segmentation approaches while recent trends point to the growing application of transformer-based and instance-segmentation strategies. However, the field is still hampered by the scarcity and poor annotation of publicly available renal datasets. Aiming to further contribute to the enhancement of the field, a dataset of 18 Whole Slide Images (WSIs) of unstained human kidney tissue is made publicly available. Additionally, in the dataset, we provide 543 annotated tiles extracted from the WSIs, facilitating further research into stain-independent segmentation approaches. As a third contribution, we present a preliminary case study, evaluating state-of-the-art deep learning segmentation architectures, including U-Net and Segment Anything Model (SAM). Our preliminary results indicate that deep learning models demonstrate promising segmentation performance in unstained kidney biopsies. In alignment with these findings, advanced customised loss functions and data augmentation were integrated into the supervised training of the promising U-Net, DeepLabv3+, and TransUNet models, achieving significant improvements compared to the baseline experiments. To exploit the abundance of unlabelled data, we further tested FixMatchSeg, a semi-supervised learning method; however, its segmentation performance remained slightly behind the supervised methods. Taken together, these contributions establish a foundation for future research in stain-independent Computational Pathology, demonstrating that unstained brightfield microscopy images can reliably support downstream tissue analysis tasks. Our dataset, validation experiments, and methodological insights provide the community with both resources and benchmarks to advance robust, data-efficient, and generalisable kidney tissue segmentation.

papers.title: QT-RelCor: Statistical Inference for Comorbidity of Quantitative Traits and Disease from Related Individuals
papers.abstract: Background: Complex diseases with a high genetic component often cluster in families and are associated with quantitative traits (QT-s) such as endophenotypes showing comorbidity with the end-point disease trait. Detecting associations with such QT-s can provide a non-invasive approach to indicate disease onset at an early stage, or help in tracking disease severity. Traditional case-control studies generally involve unrelated individuals, which can introduce heterogeneity due to varying lifestyle and exposure patterns. Often QT values may be available from related individuals such as families of affected probands. In these situations, assessment of comorbidity restricting to unrelated cases and controls leads to unnecessary loss of power. On the other hand, ignoring the correlation structure of families leads to grossly incorrect confidence intervals impacting both type 1 error and power of tests. Yet, these practices are common in the absence of standard inference procedures for such data. Methods: We propose statistical procedures for analyzing clustered data to infer association between the QT-s and the binary trait. The methods allow a mix of families and unrelated cases and utilizes all available individuals. In particular, two novel competing approaches are proposed and evaluated: a parametric approach based on multivariate normal likelihood and a non-parametric approach that combines the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with a modified version of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results: We conducted simulation studies to assess type 1 error and power across multiple scenarios, which demonstrated the robustness of the proposed tests. Both the tests perform considerably better than both the classical t-test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test under both parametric and non-parametric settings. We illustrate the proposed methods by applying them on sibship data from the Centre for Brain and Mind program to identify a number of quantitative precursors significantly associated with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Conclusion: In summary, the proposed methods provide a robust and powerful approach to detect comorbid endophenotypes incorporating data from families of affected individuals. Findings from the analysis of sibling-based data on schizophrenia and bipolar disorder support role of a few selected neurocognitive assessments as potential markers of these disorders.

papers.title: Quantum Machine Learning for Missense Variant Pathogenicity Prediction in the KCNQ Gene Family
papers.abstract: Missense variants in the KCNQ family of voltage-gated potassium channel genes are associated with a broad spectrum of neurological and cardiac disorders for which computational tools capable of differentiating benign and pathogenic variants are essential. Here, we present, to our knowledge, the first application of quantum machine learning (QML) to missense pathogenicity prediction. We employ a hybrid quantum framework combining data re-uploading quantum neural networks with quantum support vector machines and applied it to pathogenicity classification across the full KCNQ gene family. Systematic exploration of circuit architectures revealed that optimal hyperparameter choices enable the proposed quantum model to achieve predictive performance superior to or comparable to state-of-the-art classical machine learning approaches, reaching AUC-ROC values of approximately 0.94 across the full dataset. Although no clear quantum advantage is observed at present, these results demonstrate that quantum feature representations can effectively capture biologically relevant patterns in variant data and establish QML as a viable framework for future applications in computational genomics and precision medicine.

papers.title: S-PLM-TM enables fast and accurate sequence-based search for remote homologs
papers.abstract: Protein structures and functions can remain conserved after extensive sequence divergence, but detecting these distant relationships across large databases remains challenging. Here we present S-PLM-TM, a sequence-only remote homology search tool based on a structure-aware protein language model. Cross-modal flow matching and contrastive learning incorporate structural information into sequence representations. A lightweight calibration head enables structural-similarity search with the frozen encoder, while a residue-level alignment head generates structural alignments directly from sequence. S-PLM-TM outperforms the tested sequence-based methods in remote homology detection, rivals structure-based methods in structural classification and retrieves the most functionally consistent neighbors. It also retrieves distantly related enzymes with shared catalytic functions at a level comparable to the best-performing structure-based methods. In large-scale database search, S-PLM-TM achieves the highest average precision among both sequence-based and alignment-free methods, with speed approaching the fastest sequence-alignment tools. Together, these results establish S-PLM-TM as a practical tool that combines sensitive and biologically informative remote homology search with the speed required for database-scale retrieval.

papers.title: LDEN: Alternating projections for whole genome linkage disequilibrium estimation from next-generation sequencing data
papers.abstract: Viral populations often exist as quasispecies of closely-related variants with different mutations. Variants that possess combinations of mutations conferring an overall fitness advantage replicate preferentially. Understanding the true fitness effects of mutations involves disentangling the effects of individual mutations from their genetic background. This problem becomes particularly challenging due to linkage disequilibrium, the non-random association between mutations, which can cause neutral mutations to appear fit and vice versa. Viral populations are typically studied via next-generation sequencing, in which the read length is much shorter than the genome length, rendering long-range linkage disequilibrium unobservable. Estimation of linkage disequilibrium can be performed via population reconstruction, which reconstructs complete sequences before calculating linkage disequilibrium. However, this approach is computationally slow, memory-intensive, and prone to errors, particularly in regions of low coverage. In this work, we present a novel, population reconstruction-independent method for linkage disequilibrium estimation directly from next-generation sequencing data. Our approach uses the observed intra-read linkage disequilibrium values to estimate the unobservable inter-read ones by enforcing mathematical constraints on the linkage disequilibrium matrix. Specifically, because linkage disequilibrium quantifies the covariance between mutant allele frequencies, the linkage disequilibrium matrix must be positive semidefinite. We have formulated linkage disequilibrium estimation as a matrix completion problem and solve it via alternating projections on the constraints of positive semidefiniteness and observed linkage disequilibrium values. This allows the propagation of information from observed intra-read associations to the unobservable inter-read ones without reconstructing the individual variants. We demonstrate that our method yields higher accuracy while being two orders of magnitude faster compared to population reconstruction-based estimation. We demonstrate the performance of the method on both simulated as well as real data showing that it can estimate linkage disequilibrium from a variety of populations.
